fixes.explanation: Fire from heaven sounds dramatic, I'll give you that. But Micah's first picture is much softer: "…like dew from the LORD, like showers on the grass…" (Micah 5:7). Dew is gentle, and it comes from the LORD. A lion shows up in the very next verse, and that's a whole different picture.

Close, friend, but the text says the opposite. Dew and showers are "…like showers on the grass, which do not wait for man or linger for mankind." (Micah 5:7). They don't wait around for anybody. Rain has never once asked if you were ready, and I say that as someone who has left a window open.

That's right, friend. Micah says the dew and showers "…do not wait for man or linger for mankind." (Micah 5:7). They don't hang around for anybody to give permission. They just arrive, and the grass is glad about it.

Baked just right, friend! Micah says the remnant will be "…like a lion among the beasts of the forest…" (Micah 5:8). Hold up, we just had soft dew a verse ago, and now we've got a lion! Micah doesn't stay in one picture for long.

Sheep do show up in this verse, friend, but not as the remnant. Micah says the remnant is "…like a lion among the beasts of the forest, like a young lion among flocks of sheep…" (Micah 5:8). So the remnant is the lion in both pictures. Nobody here is the wolf's lunch.

A lily is pretty, friend, but it isn't in this verse. Micah says the remnant will be "…like a lion among the beasts of the forest…" (Micah 5:8). That's a big change from the soft dew in the verse before. A lily would never survive a picture like this one.

Not quite, friend. Micah says the lion goes through "…with no one to rescue them." (Micah 5:8). So the text says no one is there to rescue them. I'd want that one read twice, and the text says it plainly.

That's right, friend. In the lion picture, Micah says the lion tramples and tears as it passes through "…with no one to rescue them." (Micah 5:8). The text says no one is there to rescue them. It's a heavy picture, so I'll just let the words stand.

That's right, friend! Micah says, "Your hand will be lifted over your foes, and all your enemies will be cut off." (Micah 5:9). Notice the word "all." The text doesn't say some of them. It says all your enemies.

Making peace is a kind thought, friend, but that's not what the text says. Micah says, "Your hand will be lifted over your foes, and all your enemies will be cut off." (Micah 5:9). Peace doesn't come up in this verse. The word is cut off.

Servants is a creative guess, friend, but the text goes another way. Micah says, "Your hand will be lifted over your foes, and all your enemies will be cut off." (Micah 5:9). Nobody is put to work in this verse. All your enemies will be cut off.

Box-worthy, friend! The LORD says, "I will remove your horses from among you and wreck your chariots." (Micah 5:10). Horses and chariots go together, so He takes both. Chariots are the word that fills this blank.

Ships are a good guess for something that gets wrecked, friend, but they're not in this verse. The LORD says, "I will remove your horses from among you and wreck your chariots." (Micah 5:10). The horses come out and the chariots get wrecked. There isn't a boat in sight.

Wagons are close, friend, but they aren't the word here. The LORD says, "I will remove your horses from among you and wreck your chariots." (Micah 5:10). Chariots are what goes with the horses in this verse. A wagon is a different thing, and I'd hate to wreck the wrong one.

That's right, friend! The LORD says, "I will remove the cities of your land and tear down all your strongholds." (Micah 5:11). Both the cities and all the strongholds are named. The text doesn't leave one standing in this verse.

Not this time, friend. The text says it's true: "I will remove the cities of your land and tear down all your strongholds." (Micah 5:11). The cities and all the strongholds are both named. It's a long list, and I read it twice to be sure.

Perfect bake, friend! The LORD says, "I will cut the sorceries from your hand, and you will have no fortune-tellers." (Micah 5:12). Sorceries go and fortune-tellers go with them. That's the word for the blank.

Tax collectors would be a different kind of verse, friend. The LORD says, "I will cut the sorceries from your hand, and you will have no fortune-tellers." (Micah 5:12). Sorceries and fortune-tellers go together here. Nobody's tax bill comes up in this one.

Gatekeepers are a fair guess, friend, but they're not in this verse. The LORD says, "I will cut the sorceries from your hand, and you will have no fortune-tellers." (Micah 5:12). The sorceries go and the fortune-tellers go with them. The gate stays out of it.

That's a keeper, friend! The LORD says, "I will also cut off the carved images and sacred pillars from among you, so that you will no longer bow down to the work of your own hands." (Micah 5:13). The reason is right there in the verse. People were bowing to something their own hands made.

More room for crops is a practical thought, friend, but the verse doesn't say it. The LORD says, "I will also cut off the carved images and sacred pillars from among you, so that you will no longer bow down to the work of your own hands." (Micah 5:13). The reason given is about bowing down. It's about what their hands made, and crops aren't mentioned.

Carrying off isn't the reason in this verse, friend. The LORD says, "I will also cut off the carved images and sacred pillars from among you, so that you will no longer bow down to the work of your own hands." (Micah 5:13). The reason is the bowing down. The nations aren't part of this one.

Fine work, baker! The LORD says, "I will take vengeance in anger and wrath upon the nations that have not obeyed Me." (Micah 5:15). The text names one thing about these nations, that they have not obeyed Him. That's the whole description.

Closeness isn't what the verse talks about, friend. The LORD says, "I will take vengeance in anger and wrath upon the nations that have not obeyed Me." (Micah 5:15). The text doesn't say where these nations sit on the map. It says they have not obeyed Him.

Warnings aren't mentioned in this verse, friend, so I won't add one. The LORD says, "I will take vengeance in anger and wrath upon the nations that have not obeyed Me." (Micah 5:15). The text describes these nations by one thing only, that they have not obeyed Him.
